findings.section: AWS allows a request only when nothing denies and something allows
findings.quote: Now follow one request through four checks. Use them as a checklist: the result is the same in any order.
findings.evidence: Fact iam-eval-deny-checked-first: 'The enforcement code first looks for a Deny statement in every policy that applies' and 'If there is no explicit deny, the enforcement code evaluation continues.' The order decides which kind of deny she names, and the chapter teaches her to name it (case table: 'Implicit deny' vs 'Explicit deny'). Example: an SCP leaves the action out AND an identity-based policy has a Deny. If she checks the ceiling first and stops, she answers 'implicit deny'; AWS returns an explicit deny. The sentence also contradicts the subsection's own figure (a ladder that starts with the deny question) and has no fact link (hard rule 1). Fix: 'Check the deny first, as AWS does; then the ceilings and the grant.' This also cuts words.
findings.resolution: The 'same in any order' sentence is deleted; the four checks follow the figure, deny first (claims-002).

findings.section: Condition keys narrow an allow to the right organization or network
findings.quote: 2. **Missing key.** If the request does not carry the key, [the condition is false](../facts/iam.md#iam-condition-missing-key-is-false-except-ifexists). ... (Spot the bug answer) when the request comes through a VPC endpoint the key is not available, so NotIpAddress is true. Exempt aws:SourceVpce too.
findings.evidence: Fact iam-condition-missing-key-is-false-except-ifexists, source docs/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators: 'If the policy condition requires that the key is *not* matched, such as `StringNotLike` or `ArnNotLike`, and the right key is not present, the condition is *true*.' The trap edit removed the sentence 'A negated operator turns this around', so step 2 now states the rule as absolute, and 30 lines later the Spot-the-bug answer says the opposite (missing key, condition true) with no reason. A reader who applies step 2 concludes that the Deny does not apply and that the instances are fine, which is the bug the exercise is meant to teach. Fix: add to step 2 'For a negated operator, such as NotIpAddress or StringNotLike, a missing key makes the condition true.' In the answer, write the fix as a full sentence: 'Add a condition so that the Deny does not apply to requests from the VPC endpoint (aws:SourceVpce).'
findings.resolution: Step 2 adds the negated-operator case (claims-001). The Spot the bug answer is kept as written for word budget.

findings.section: Condition keys narrow an allow to the right organization or network (Stop and answer)
findings.quote: **Stop and answer.** A bucket policy allows s3:DeleteObject when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true. A script deletes with an IAM user's access key. Can it delete? ... No: [long-term access keys do not include it]
findings.evidence: Fact iam-eval-same-account-identity-or-resource-allow: 'If an action is allowed by an identity-based policy, a resource-based policy, or both, then AWS allows the action.' The stem does not say what the user's own IAM policy allows. If the user is in the bucket's account and the user's policy allows s3:DeleteObject (the usual case, and the exact setup of quiz Question 16: 'Their IAM policy allows all Amazon S3 actions'), the delete succeeds, because a false condition only switches off that one Allow. The answer 'No' teaches the wrong model that a conditional Allow restricts access. The subsection heading 'Condition keys narrow an allow' supports the same wrong model; to enforce TLS, MFA or a VPC endpoint, a policy uses a Deny with the condition (fact iam-faq-restrict-with-deny-statement: 'To restrict access, specify a Deny statement in any policy.'). Fix: add 'The user's own policies say nothing about Amazon S3' to the stem, and add one line to the subsection: 'An Allow with a condition only removes that one Allow. To enforce a rule, put the condition on a Deny.'
findings.resolution: Same fix as claims-003: stem says the user's own policies say nothing about Amazon S3; the answer says to enforce MFA with a Deny.

findings.section: Decision record; The root user and IAM users hold long-term credentials (trap); data/03-iam/speak.json iam-s04; 5-quiz.md Question 9

findings.section: A permissions boundary lets developers create roles without escalating

findings.section: A KMS key policy decides whether IAM policies count for the key
findings.quote: Why does the key policy decide? The key protects the data, so its owner says yes on the key itself. ... Can the role read an S3 object that this key encrypts (SSE-KMS)? ... No.
findings.evidence: Rule: a mechanism stated without cause and effect. 'SSE-KMS' is never expanded or explained. The 'Why' sentence gives no real cause, because one account owns both the key and the IAM policy. The answer is now a bare 'No.' with the reasoning moved into a trap bullet, and the causal chain is still missing: to return the object, Amazon S3 asks AWS KMS to decrypt on behalf of the role; the key policy neither names the role nor enables IAM policies; so AWS KMS denies, and GetObject fails. She cannot reason through Question 13 from this text.
findings.resolution: Partial: the stem expands SSE-KMS and names the key policy state; the Why line now cites AWS ('AWS calls the key policy [the primary way to control access]'). The causal chain (Amazon S3 asks AWS KMS for the same principal) is in the answer's trap bullet.

The text does not say what happens next: your role trusts the vendor's account, so the vendor assumes your role for the other customer and shows that customer your data. The external ID breaks this, because the other customer's ID is different. The quoted definition ('coerces a more privileged entity') is abstract English for a second-language reader. Add one sentence with the concrete consequence.

findings.section: iam-t01 (1-fast.md Look first)
findings.quote: "kills": "\"A role has its own password or access key.\"" ... "Pick one role name from the list as <ROLE_NAME>. Read its trust policy and look for a password or a key." ... "expect": "A JSON document with Effect, Principal and Action sts:AssumeRole. No password and no key."
findings.evidence: Rule: a task must kill the belief that it names. A trust policy is a policy document; it never holds a password or a key, for a user or for a role. So finding none proves nothing about whether a role has long-term credentials. A step that does test the belief: compare the ARN from get-caller-identity in CloudShell (an assumed-role ARN, which means temporary credentials) with the role's JSON, or run 'aws iam list-access-keys' with a role name and read the error. findings.section: iam-s01, iam-s02
findings.quote: (s01) "You attach the role to the worker's instance through an instance profile." ... (s02) "A bucket policy keeps the job in its own account. A role moves it into the other account." ... "In your case, the job copies files into its own bucket."
findings.evidence: Rule: a spoken answer must sound like speech and stay correct. In s01, 'worker' appears without introduction; the prompt says 'the code on the instance'. In s02, 'moves it into the other account' is a metaphor that a listener can take literally; say 'with a role, the job acts as a role of the other account'. 'In your case, the job copies files' invents a fact that the prompt does not give; make it a condition ('If the job copies files into its own bucket ...').
findings.resolution: iam-s01: 'worker' replaced by 'the instance', 'the code' and 'the application'; iam-s02: ten_second says 'A bucket policy keeps the job's own permissions. With a role, it acts as the other account's role.', and 'In your case, if the job copies into its own bucket, use the bucket policy.'

findings.section: How it works: Say it lines
findings.quote: > **Say it:** The short answer is: allow or deny, which actions, on which resources. The thing to watch is a broad AWS managed policy.
findings.evidence: Rule: Say it lines are written for speech. All 14 subsection Say it lines use the same frame 'The short answer is: ... The thing to watch is ...'. Several are noun fragments ('allow or deny, which actions, on which resources'; 'The thing to watch is a broad AWS managed policy') that do not work as spoken sentences. Keep the frame for some and write the others as full sentences ('Watch out for broad AWS managed policies: they give more than the task needs').
findings.resolution: STYLE.md section 5 and SPEC.json (label Say it) require the frame 'The short answer is ... The thing to watch is'.

findings.section: Question 1 (iam-q004) Think aloud step 5
findings.quote: My first idea breaks because the role and the bucket are in different accounts, so both accounts must allow the read; the bucket is in account B and the role is in account A, so I also choose the identity-based policy of the role.
findings.evidence: STYLE: short sentences. One sentence of about 45 words with two 'so' clauses and a semicolon, and it repeats the account facts. Split it: 'My first idea breaks. The role and the bucket are in different accounts, so both accounts must allow the read. I also choose the role's identity-based policy.'
findings.resolution: Step 5 of iam-q004 split into two sentences; it keeps the wrong-path marker 'My first idea breaks because' that Q114 requires.

findings.section: Question 17 (iam-q023), Question 9 (iam-q020), Question 2 (iam-q001)
findings.quote: (Q17) "A role gives the vendor temporary credentials.The external ID is" ... "an access key would [remain valid until you manually revoke them]" ... (Q9) "AWS advises to [require MFA for additional security]" ... (Q2) "so the certificate authority is bait"
findings.evidence: STYLE plain English. Q17: no space after the period; 'an access key ... them' mixes singular and plural (write 'access keys would remain valid until you manually revoke them'). Q9: 'advises to' is ungrammatical; use 'AWS recommends that you'. Q2: 'bait' is an idiom; use 'does not matter here'. Edit in questions.json.
findings.resolution: iam-q023: space added and 'access keys would remain valid'; iam-q020: 'AWS recommends that you'; iam-q001 worked step: 'does not matter here'.

findings.section: A policy statement pairs an effect with actions and resources
findings.quote: | Kind | Attach to many identities? | ... | Customer managed | Yes, with [up to five versions] |
findings.evidence: The column question is 'Attach to many identities?', but the cells answer other questions (can you change it, how many versions). A skim gives no reason to choose one kind over another. Use columns such as 'Who writes it', 'Can you edit it', 'Reuse'. The default version that the Stop-and-answer needs (reader-18) could be one cell here.
findings.resolution: Note; no word room: 2-deep.md is at its XL cap (5,498 of 5,500 words after this fix).

findings.section: The root user and IAM users hold long-term credentials
findings.quote: 3. **IAM user.** A user can have [two access keys](../facts/iam.md#iam-access-keys-max-two-per-user), so a rotation uses the second one.
findings.evidence: Rule: a mechanism without cause and effect. 'A rotation uses the second one' skips the steps that make two keys useful: create the second key, move the applications to it, deactivate the first key, then delete it. The Numbers table repeats the same short form ('Rotation uses the second key slot').
findings.resolution: Note; no word room: 2-deep.md is at its XL cap (5,498 of 5,500 words after this fix).

findings.section: Decision record; In the real world
findings.quote: **Context.** A customer's purchase form asks who can access the recordings. ... **It shows:** permission sets put least privilege into practice.
findings.evidence: Lint W201: 'Decision record has 356 words; the section allows 0 to 280'. The numbered lists under both figures repeat the figure alt text and the captions almost word for word; cut one of each pair (this also frees words under the XL cap). 'Purchase form' is unclear; say 'a customer's security questionnaire'. 'In the real world' gives one quote and a one-line lesson that adds nothing beyond the Identity Center subsection, and 'a specific list of attributes' is unexplained. Name one concrete thing Navan did with permission sets, or cut it.
findings.resolution: 'Purchase form' is the story's trigger (data/startup.json); the numbered lists under the figures must equal the spec steps (L703). The Decision line lost one sentence, but the section is still over 280 words (W201 warning).

findings.section: Changed recently (root MFA)
findings.quote: > **Old:** management and standalone accounts required root user MFA; member accounts did not.
findings.evidence: Fact iam-root-mfa-required-all-account-types (What's New quote): 'requiring MFA for AWS Organizations management account root users in May 2024, followed by expanding MFA requirements to standalone account root users in June 2024'. The 'Old' line describes only the 2024-2025 state. Questions written since mid-2022 can assume no root MFA requirement for any account type (the fact's note: 'Older exam questions treat root MFA as a best practice, not a requirement'). Write the old value as 'before May 2024, no account type required root MFA'.
findings.resolution: Partial: 'The exam probably expects' now says 'older questions treat it as optional'. The Old line stays: it is the value of `changed.was` of iam-root-mfa-required-all-account-types for the 2025-06-17 change.

findings.section: In one breath (Startup example); 2-deep.md Decision record
findings.quote: > **Startup example:** Callvale's application calls Amazon S3 and Amazon Transcribe with the root user's access key. The key is stored in the code. Ana and Ben share the root user's password.
findings.evidence: STARTUP.md introduces Ana (CEO, co-founder) and Ben (CTO, co-founder). Chapter 03 is the first story chapter that the reader opens in the study order (security first), and neither file says who Callvale, Ana and Ben are. Add 'Callvale, a call-analysis startup, and its two founders, Ana and Ben' once in the Startup example.
findings.resolution: Startup example now reads 'Callvale, a call-intelligence startup, ... The founders, Ana and Ben, share ...'.

findings.section: How it works (repeated sentences)
findings.quote: [remain valid until you manually revoke them] (lines 151 and 167) ... [does not have standard long-term credentials, such as a password or access keys] (169 and 349) ... [the permissions are not cumulative] (179 and 211) ... [cannot identify a user group as a principal] (75 and 295) ... [does not provide permissions on its own] (99 and 480) ... [allowed by both its identity-based policies and its permissions boundaries] (132 and 457) ... [does not give up its permissions] (269 and 272)
findings.evidence: Orchestrator note: the deep file is 10 words under its XL cap, so fixes that add words need cuts. These seven fact phrases each appear twice within a few subsections, and FAQ 6, 7, 9 and 10 repeat body sentences word for word. They are the cheapest cuts for the words that reader-01, reader-05, reader-06, reader-12 and reader-32 need. Keep the first occurrence in the subsection that teaches the fact.
findings.resolution: Cut the duplicate sentences: the long-term key line at the top of the role subsection, 'the permissions are not cumulative' in the contractor answer, the second 'does not give up its permissions' in the exam signal, the boundary sentence in the developer-role answer and the trusted-account sentence in the SQS answer.

findings.section: FAQ quick-fire, FAQ 2
findings.quote: **FAQ 2.** Does an empty SCP on an account allow every action? ... No. It is [equivalent to attaching a policy that explicitly denies all actions].
findings.evidence: The body teaches that an SCP which leaves an action out gives an implicit deny (case table, case 3; 1-fast Predict 1). FAQ 2 then says that an empty SCP is like an explicit deny of everything, with no word on why the two differ. A reader who 'acts before she reads' will mix the two up. One clause is enough: 'An empty SCP allows nothing, so every action is blocked; no allow can fix it.'
findings.resolution: Note; no word room: 2-deep.md is at its XL cap (5,498 of 5,500 words after this fix).
